title: Getting out of your comfort zone

posts.topic_title: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.author: MichaelH
posts.post_subject: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.content_md:
I hadn't really intended my [last post on DCG](http://holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=5054) to become a discussion about the merits of SBR work vs multi-beam mastering and copying but since it has, I'll attempt to resurrect the question I posed in a different thread.

> What would take to get you out of your comfort zone? What do you need in order to try something new that other people "know" would make a difference in how your holograms turn out?

For me it would really be nice to have another couple of days off in the week where I can do whatever I want, all day long with no place I have to be or anyone I have to interact with. Just another day or two to spend all day long in the lab. I'd set aside at least one of these days for pure experimentation without a need to produce anything. Just spend time making attempts at whatever with only the results (success or failure) to show for it.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.post_subject: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Definitely time!!!!!!

Ok, we'd probably be doing it if we had all the time we wanted. Or would we? It's a well known maxim that work expands to fill the time allotted so maybe another couple of days would just be eaten up with more holograms made the same way.

Instead of just asking for more time (which I'd like anyway) I wonder if I could make the following rule work.

Every X hologram (2nd, 3rd, whatever, but something regular) should be made with some part of the process changed. Changing chemistry, film, laser, whatever. Something boundary stretching. 

After exploring that change, the next hologram can be made with the tried-and-true method or the change can become part of the "normal" process and used for the next hologram.

I'll have to give more thought into how I can do this.

posts.topic_title: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.content_md:
> Or would we?

I would as I do it now. I have decided mostly not to go the production side of holography except for a few jobs to people I know personally. 

As you have seen in most of my documentation over the past few years I have tried quite a bit. For me that's where the fun is, trying new stuff. It wasn't really accepted when I tried to ask for advise about doing something insanely different so I have stopped. I just go in the lab and whatever is jiggling around in my head, I try. To me that is the creative part of holography not the trying to figure out what is creative so someone else will want it and buy it. I get a lot of failures in the begining and I guess that's why I love DCG. It allows me to expose a 5x7 plate for tesing which only costs me pennies (with reusing the glass). Can you imaging not being concerned with cost (other then time). It helps a lot. I guess that's why I need more time...

Things I have tried;

Mirrors in hologram to include reflection of image with image.

H1 Silver to H2 DCG.

Refection H1 DCG to H2 DCG.

Multiple geometries (some very novel).

Multi color.

On axis hologram.

Abstract.

Holographic microscopy.

Color tuning.

Broadband (not yellow but white reflection hologams).

Alternate fixing, hardening, gelatin fabrication, coating techniques.

Difficult objects (ice cube).

Multi exposure (same and different wavelength).

Single beam, split beam, assisted lighting.

Dual reference beams

Post finished hologram wavelength shifting

etc...

I totally recommend trying something new and different if you are in it for the fun and not trying to make money at it!

posts.topic_title: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.content_md:
I've had good results with a spherical mirror, too. The larger the mirror, the better (if the narrow beam spread is acceptable in your setup) since you have more areas in which to find a clean spot. The same would hold true for a lens. I've had some very clean beams from a lens alone (as I recall, pretty much perfect). But the key parameter is having a larger lens or spherical mirror, so that a clean spot can be found somewhere. 

I have often wondered if the spatial filter can be dispensed with for two or three-color holograms, since it's even more aggravating to use in that case. If a lens or mirror will work to spread the combined beams, then color holography would be a lot easier, and maybe more people would be doing it. I would think that if multiple co-linear beams were adjusted properly (diameter and divergence) then a lens or mirror could be used to spread the reference beam. I haven't seen this documented, though, and there may be a problem of which I'm unaware.

posts.topic_title: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Getting out of your comfort zone
posts.content_md:
> If a lens or mirror will work to spread the combined beams, then color holography would be a lot easier, and maybe more people would be doing it.

I doubt it. Of the very small number of people making holograms, those making multi-color holograms (or wanting to) have much bigger fish to fry than worrying about aligning spatial filters. 

The mirrors and dichroics used to steer and combine the beams will put more noise into the beams. Finding a "good spot" on the spreading optic will not help with that. Also, the cost of multiple lasers, the panchromatic film (think about all that experimentation to get the colors right), and the cost of all the tilters and mounts to combine the beams require a budget so high that a spatial filter is not a big deal. 

Sure, diverging a beam with a simple lens or spherical mirror works just fine for many systems. Its use will, however, only mean the holographer will be fiddling with *that* instead of the spatial filter!
